name: TCA CROSS

card.summary: Dermatologist-applied pinpoint dabs of high-strength acid into icepick scars; small trials report improvement, with no large controlled evidence.
card.aka: Chemical reconstruction of skin scars; CROSS technique
card.note: Trials are small and mostly open-label; the procedure is clinician-performed.

quick.overview:
TCA CROSS (chemical reconstruction of skin scars) is a dermatology procedure in which a clinician applies a high concentration of trichloroacetic acid to the base of individual atrophic acne scars, most often narrow icepick scars, rather than peeling the whole face.

Published studies, mostly small and many without a control group, report meaningful improvement in scar appearance after a series of sessions. Head-to-head trials against subcision, microneedling and pinpoint CO2 laser have produced mixed comparisons.
quick.mechanism: The acid is applied focally to the depressed scar and is thought to cause a controlled injury in the dermis, which authors propose triggers new collagen formation and lifts the scar floor. Studies describe this as dermal thickening rather than resurfacing of the surrounding skin.
quick.risks: The original authors reported no significant complications in a 65-patient series. Concentrations used in studies range from 50% to 100%; it is a clinician-performed procedure and acid at these strengths is not an over-the-counter product.

lead: TCA CROSS, short for chemical reconstruction of skin scars, is a dermatologic technique for atrophic (depressed) acne scars in which a clinician applies a high-concentration trichloroacetic acid (TCA) solution to individual scars rather than to the whole face. It was described by Korean authors in a 2002 report on patients with dark skin types [1].

It is most associated with icepick scars and deep, narrow boxcar scars, which are described in dermatology literature as hard to improve with whole-face resurfacing [2][7]. Published studies use concentrations from 50% to 100% and typically repeat sessions every few weeks [1][3][4][5].

The evidence consists mostly of small prospective or retrospective series, with a few randomised comparisons against other scar treatments. A 2017 systematic review examined the efficacy and adverse reactions of non-energy-based acne scar treatments [6]. Review authors have noted that few randomised trials exist to identify any single gold-standard approach to acne scarring [10].
infobox: Atrophic acne scars, esp. icepick and boxcar

paras: Acne scars are commonly classified as icepick, boxcar and rolling types, a classification proposed in a 2001 review that also set out a treatment algorithm including punch techniques, subcision and laser resurfacing [2]. Icepick scars are narrow (generally under 2 mm) and extend into the dermis [7].

In TCA CROSS, as described in the original report, the acid is applied by pressing on the depressed area of the scar rather than spreading it across the skin, so the surrounding tissue is largely spared [1]. Procedural details such as applicator choice, number of passes and aftercare vary between clinicians and are not covered here.

sections.h: How it is thought to work
paras: The original authors proposed that the focal high-strength acid injures the scar tissue in a controlled way, prompting new collagen deposition that raises the base of the scar [1]. A later comparative study describes the method's advantage as reconstructing scars by increasing dermal thickening and collagen production [8]. Histology in one small series examined samples from two patients' back scars [4].

The 2002 series compared 65% and 100% TCA [1]. A 2008 report examined 50% TCA, as opposed to the roughly 90% used in earlier work, with the stated aim of reducing local adverse effects [4]. A 2015 study evaluated 70% TCA in 53 patients [5].

In the 2002 case series of 65 patients with Fitzpatrick skin types IV-V, 82% of the 65% TCA group and 94% of the 100% TCA group were reported to have a good clinical response, and the authors reported no significant complications [1].
A randomised study of 30 participants compared four sessions of percutaneous collagen induction (microneedling) with four sessions of 100% TCA CROSS and reported improvement in both groups [8].

A split-face comparison in 20 patients with rolling scars (skin types III-IV) found that subcision produced significantly greater reduction in scar size and depth than 100% TCA CROSS, with fewer side effects, although scar depth continued to decrease over time after CROSS [11].
A 2014 randomised pilot study of 28 patients with icepick scars compared pinpoint CO2 laser irradiation with TCA CROSS and reported greater improvement with the laser [12].

In a 2015 study of 53 patients, 66% had good or excellent improvement (over 50%) on physician and patient assessments after 70% TCA CROSS, and 81.1% were satisfied or very satisfied; outcomes were better in patients with predominantly boxcar scars and higher baseline severity [5].

A five-patient report of 50% TCA described improvement in depth and appearance of scars on the face and back [4]. A registered trial comparing subcision followed by diluted calcium hydroxylapatite injection with subcision followed by TCA CROSS has been completed with 13 participants; no results are listed in the registry entry [13].

The original 2002 report stated there were no significant complications [1], and a 2015 study concluded 70% TCA was safe in all atrophic scar types [5]. The subcision comparison reported more side effects with 100% TCA CROSS than with subcision [11]. Pigmentation change is a commonly discussed concern with chemical peeling in general; the original series was conducted in patients with Fitzpatrick skin types IV-V [1]. Because studies differ in how they record adverse events and are small, rates are not firmly established.

TCA CROSS is categorised on the wiki under hardmaxx, the community's term for invasive or procedural interventions. The entry was added because of its use for icepick scars; no forum threads are cited in this article.

timeline.event: A classification system for acne scars and treatment algorithm is published [2].
CROSS technique reported in a 65-patient series in dark-complexioned patients [1].
Randomised comparisons with microneedling and subcision are published [8][11].
Pilot trial compares CROSS with pinpoint CO2 laser for icepick scars [12].
